Chapter 9: Personal Reckoning
For anyone who lived through the genocide—whether they were survivors, peacekeepers, or aid workers—coming to terms with what happened is something deeply personal.
The memories? They're vivid, sometimes overwhelming, but in a strange way, they can also open the door to growth and understanding.
Take, for example, a retired peacekeeper who now spends his days volunteering at a community center. He sits with young people, sharing what he’s been through—the lessons he learned, and even the mistakes he made along the way.
These conversations can be tough and honest, but they build real connections. And in those moments, hope starts to take root.
Then there's a survivor, someone who’s become a leader in her community. She organizes support groups for people still wrestling with trauma. She listens, she offers advice, and she helps them find a way forward.
Her own story is marked by pain and loss, but it’s also a testament to resilience and determination.
Here’s something to remember: personal reckoning looks different for everyone. Some people find comfort in faith. Others throw themselves into activism or express themselves through art.
Many wrestle with guilt—whether it’s survivor’s guilt, or the ache of not having been able to do more. Healing never moves in a straight line, and setbacks? They’re part of the journey.
Picture this: one evening, a group of former peacekeepers gets together for a reunion. They swap stories, laugh about the old days, and then fall quiet when talk turns to Rwanda.
The camaraderie is still there, but so is the heavy awareness of all they’ve lost. That experience changed them in ways they’re still trying to grasp.
And for so many, the most important lesson is this: we have to bear witness. We need to remember, to speak out, and to act when we see others in danger.
The story of Rwanda reminds us—every choice we make, every action we take, really does matter. The responsibility to prevent future atrocities? That belongs to all of us.
